title: Patching the screens
translation: Hōjō Tokiyori, who ran the government in Kamakura, had a mother called the nun Matsushita. Once, when she was expecting a visit from him, she was mending the sooty paper screens herself, cutting out just the torn squares with a little knife and pasting in new paper. Her brother Yoshikage, who was helping with the arrangements that day, said, "Let me give that to one of the men. He's good at that sort of thing."
"He won't do it any better than I can," she said, and went on pasting, one square at a time.
Yoshikage tried again. "It would be much easier to redo the whole thing. And doesn't a patchwork look a bit shabby?"
"I'll redo it all properly later. But today I want it like this, on purpose. I want the young people to see it and learn: when something tears, you mend the torn part and keep using it."

That was remarkable. Running a country starts with not wasting things. She was a woman, but she thought like a sage. She raised a son who held the whole country in his hands. No ordinary woman, people say.

literal: The mother of Tokiyori, Governor of Sagami, was called the Zen nun Matsushita.
When there was an occasion of receiving the Governor (as a guest), she was cutting around only the torn parts of the sooty paper screens with a small knife with her own hands and pasting (them), so
her brother, Yoshikage, the Castle Officer, who was serving as the manager of that day, (said) 'Let me have it, and I will have such-and-such a man paste it.
He is a person who knows such work', he said, and
saying 'That man will surely not be better than this nun's handiwork', she still pasted one section at a time; and
Yoshikage said again, 'To replace all of it would be far easier.
Is it not unsightly to be patchy, too?', and
'This nun, too, thinks to replace it all neatly later, but today alone it should be like this on purpose.
It is to let young people see and learn that with things, you repair only the torn places and use them, and to make them aware', she said: that was very rare.
The way of governing the world takes thrift as its basis.
Though a woman, she shared the mind of a sage.
That she had as her son a person who held the realm: truly she was not an ordinary person, they say.

notes.text: Hōjō Tokiyori (1227–1263), regent ({執権|しつけん}) of the Kamakura shogunate, and in practice the ruler of the country. {相模守|さがみのかみ}: Governor of Sagami, one of his official titles.
Tokiyori's mother, a daughter of the Adachi family who became a nun after her husband's death. {禅尼|ぜんに}: a nun, here a woman of rank who had taken vows. The edition reads まつしたのぜんに.
{障子|しやうじ}: a sliding screen of paper on a wooden lattice, which lets light in. Each square of the lattice ({一間|ひとま}) can be patched on its own.
{兄|せうと}: 'brother' (of a woman). Adachi Yoshikage (1210–1253). {城介|じやうのすけ}: an official post connected with Akita castle in the north, held by the Adachi family.
A false friend: {経営|けいめい} here means looking after guests and arranging an event, as the 1925 edition explains. Modern {経営|けいえい} is 'business management'.

notes.quote: なにがし男に張らせ候はむ
notes.text: {候|さうら}ふ: polite 'to be', also used as a polite auxiliary. Yoshikage speaks to his sister politely. なにがし: 'so-and-so', a name not given.

notes.quote: 尼が細工によも勝り侍らじ
notes.text: よも … じ: 'surely not'. She calls herself {尼|あま}, 'this nun', instead of 'I'.

notes.quote: 物は破れたる所ばかりを修理して用ゐることぞ
notes.text: The lesson she wants to teach, stated as a rule. {若|わか}き{人|ひと}: 'young people'. {修理|しゆり}: the edition's reading; modern Japanese reads it しゅうり.

notes.quote: 世を治むる道、倹約を本とす
notes.text: {倹約|けんやく}: thrift, a Confucian virtue for rulers. {聖人|せいじん} in the next sentence is the Confucian sage, not a Buddhist saint.

notes.quote: ただ人にはあらざりけるとぞ
notes.text: The section ends on とぞ, 'so it is said'. The praise of the mother is passed on as something people say.
